P1.evidence: The open was the call. First line after the audio check was a remark on the prospect's posture — 'Seems like you're a little bit laid out, is that correct?' — repeated verbatim when the prospect said 'Sorry?'. No four-part frame; the only framing given was duration, delivered as a warning: 'usually you need to take like 40, 45 minutes. I don't know if you want to hold up your phone for the whole time.' No agreement sought. The scripted open question, 'what are you potentially looking for help with', was never asked at any point in five minutes. The application was referenced only as a rebuttal — 'I said you wanted to get your athletic body back. Is it not worth your time?'

P2.evidence: Only the injury check got any traction, and only because the prospect volunteered the cycle in answer to a different question. 'Why do you feel like you need a more functional workout routine then?' produced 'Because I get injured every time I work out', and the rep followed with one clarifier. He never asked what the injuries are, where, how severe, or how long it has been going on — and said so himself in the review afterwards: 'I was going to ask her right after this.' The one question aimed at occupation was aimed at something else — 'Have you had your own business or something before?' was probing his experience of sales calls, not his work.

P3.evidence: One attempt at the bridge, and it was the best question on the call: 'was there something in your life that sort of happened to you, but like, okay, now I just need to get my... together?' The prospect started to answer, the audio broke, the rep said 'I think you have your pinky on your microphone', the prospect gave a truncated 'I got injured, so I'm tired of getting injured' — and the rep ended the call fifteen seconds later. Nothing else in this phase was attempted.

P4.evidence: 'What got your interest specifically with kettlebells?' and 'You said you've been a part of these things before... take me through it' are past-attempt questions but were aimed at the sales-process objection rather than at his training history. The rep did state the root-cause logic out loud — 'we can give you a routine, but if you can[not] stick to it, then you're still going to get injured' — which is the right idea, but he asserted it rather than asking, so the prospect never named the gap himself.

P5.evidence: Call terminated at 00:05:13, long before any consequence work was reachable.

P6.evidence: Nothing was being presented, so no commitment was sought.

P11.evidence: No close attempted and no price named.

objection_plays.detail: Script gap, and a common one for inbound offers: 'I feel like if we're just going to do like a whole big sales pitch and the whole thing, like, I'm really not interested', followed by 'anything you buy online now, it seems to kind of go like this.' This is a prospect pre-loaded against the sales process itself, not against the price, the programme or his own capability. None of the five plays address it — OE is fear of the outcome, not distrust of the seller. The rep had one clean opening ('I've been a part of these things') to ask what happened last time and never took it. Instead he argued the process was necessary and twice offered to end the call.

Second unscripted trigger, ninety seconds in: an objection to the length of the call. 'Oh, it's that long?' → 'Yeah, I'm probably gonna pass, then.' There is no play for a prospect who balks at the meeting format before discovery has started. The rep pre-empted the objection by raising the duration himself, then answered the balk with 'You don't need to do it if you don't want to' — handing over the exit before any value existed to weigh against it.

notes: Not a fit problem, a first-sixty-seconds problem — and the rep's own colleague reached the same conclusion reviewing it the same day. Three things to fix in order: open with the scripted question instead of a comment on how the prospect is sitting; stop offering the exit, which was handed over twice before a single discovery question had been asked; and when a prospect says he has been through these calls before, treat it as a past-attempts question to run rather than an argument to win. The one genuinely good moment — the 'what happened in your life' bridge — arrived four minutes too late to matter.
